name: Jamal Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Jamal, and thanks for making time. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy brake pads, filters, batteries and wiper blades for Northgate Auto Parts, which sells to independent garages across three counties. Mornings I look at what the garages ordered, then I phone the makers and agents to get the best price and a delivery date. I keep a paper catalogue next to the screen, because the screen is wrong about a third of the time. I'm still the new man on the desk after five years, and Gary Platt (the manager) tells me so.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What happens when the system gets it wrong?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the phone work, and a good price that I've talked down myself. What gets to me is the rush. Every garage wants the part yesterday, and when the system says it's in stock and it isn't, I'm the one they shout at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say I told you so, though not too loudly. To friends I'd say it's the usual story: a lot of noise and then it fizzles out. I wouldn't put anything online, since I don't have the patience for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, it's no relief. Cars still need brake pads, but the garages that buy them are closing faster than the screens ever could. Half my customers are being squeezed by the chains and the electric cars.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going just as I am, with the paper catalogue and my calls to the makers. I'd keep the heating low and cut the Sunday roast out when the kids visit. And I'd ask Gary whether there's any overtime on the stocktake, because every bit helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels grey. Nothing's tragic, but there's no light at the end either. I wake up some mornings thinking about money before I think about anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen at home if Northgate shrank?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maureen, my partner, works at the laundry in a care home. Her wage is more reliable than mine, so she keeps us afloat. If Northgate shrank, we'd get through a month and no more, and I'd have to look at the benefit forms, which I'd hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the garages are closing. What does that mean for your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the thing I do know is that the firm is shaky regardless of AI. Two of our biggest garages went under last year. If it goes, it'll be the market that kills it, but the screens will get the blame.

say: I'd say **I told you so** at work, though not too loudly.
I'd tell friends it's the usual story: a lot of noise and then it **fizzles**.
think: It's no relief, because the **garages** that buy from us are closing.
The chains and electric cars are squeezing **half my customers**.
do: **Keep** the paper catalogue and my calls to the makers.
**Cut** the Sunday roast and keep the heating low.
**Ask** Gary about overtime on the stocktake.
feel: **Grey**, with no light at the end, and money on my mind first thing.
S0.quote: Cars still need brake pads, but the garages that buy them are closing faster than the screens ever could.
fieldNote: The plateau doesn't comfort him; the firm's own weak market keeps him anxious.
He distrusts the **screens** and blames the market, but expects the screens to take the blame.
His partner's care-home wage is the household's real support.

steps.text: Keep using the paper catalogue and phoning the makers
Cut the Sunday roast and keep the heating low

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's see it proven before we throw people out. To friends I'd say they're always telling us it's a revolution and it's never the bosses who pay for it. I'd say sensible folks should be asked before big changes are made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'm done. Ordering and checking prices is what the card says goes first, and I don't use any of it. I've never touched those AI tools, and at 58 I'm not going to be the one who gets good at them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably ask Gary for a position on the trade counter, which is hands-on and face to face. I'd try anything small, maybe a short course at the college if the firm pays. And I'd put 30 a week by, which is all I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like waiting for the dentist. I know it's coming and I know it will hurt, and nothing I do now changes that. I've been steady all my working life and it doesn't count for much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel about asking Winston, who is much younger, to show you the basics?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Winston at the counter is 24 and quick with the screens. I'd feel jealous and a bit sorry for myself. But I'd ask him to show me the basics, because I've got a better chance if I learn something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your boss told you the buying was moving to software, what would you ask?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they sat me down and said the buying is being done by software, I'd ask when. I'd want a date and a figure for what they'd pay me. Then at least I'd know where I stand and could tell Maureen straight.

say: I'd say let's see it **proven** before throwing people out.
I'd tell friends it's never the **bosses** who pay for the revolution.
think: I think I'm **done**, since ordering and price-checking go first and I don't use any of it.
At 58, I won't be the one who gets **good** at the tools.
do: **Ask** Gary for a job on the trade counter.
**Try** a short college course if the firm pays.
**Put** 30 a week aside, which is all I've got.
feel: Like waiting for the **dentist**, knowing it will hurt and I can't stop it.
S1.quote: I've been steady all my working life and it doesn't count for much.
fieldNote: He expects to lose the buying job and says so flatly: **alarmed**, though he sounds weary.
Pride is the barrier to learning from a 24-year-old, but he gets past it.
Wants a date and a figure from his boss, a pragmatic way to regain control.

steps.text: Ask Gary for a position on the trade counter
Take a short college course if Northgate pays
Put 30 a week aside, whatever else gives

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mad to let it go this fast. At work I'd ask what the plan is, and I suspect there won't be one. To friends I'd say the government should take it more seriously than a few headlines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's the end of the road for me. I haven't got savings, I'm not good with these tools, and there's no other job around that's like mine. Two years is the length of a bad winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd see my union rep, though we're not many, and I'd ask about redundancy pay. I'd cut my spending right down and cancel the van insurance on Theo's old car. And I'd look at claiming my pension at 60, even at a lower rate, because something is better than nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like the ground going out. I've always been the sensible one, the one who says it'll work out. This time I can't say that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your son Theo about work at his depot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My son Theo drives lorries, and he says even that's on a clock. I'd ask him if there's any warehouse work going at his depot. I'd hate it. A father shouldn't have to go to his son for work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd just go in each morning and wait. What would you be waiting for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm honest, I'd just go in each morning and wait. I wouldn't know what else to do. It's not brave and it's not smart, but it's what I'd do.

say: I'd say it's **mad** to let it go this fast.
I'd tell friends the government should take it more seriously than a few **headlines**.
think: It's the **end of the road** for me, with no savings and no similar job nearby.
Two years is the length of a **bad winter**.
do: **See** my union rep and ask about redundancy pay.
**Cut** spending right down and cancel the insurance on Theo's old car.
feel: Like the **ground going out**, because I'm usually the one who says it will work out.
S2.quote: A father shouldn't have to go to his son for work.
fieldNote: He expects the end of his job and has no plan beyond **waiting**, close to panicked but not quite.
Pride is the sore point, especially asking his son for work.
His pragmatism shows in the pension question and the redundancy query.

steps.text: See the union rep and ask about redundancy pay
Cancel the insurance on Theo's old car and cut all extras
Ask the pension office about claiming at 60 at a lower rate
Ask my son Theo about warehouse work at his depot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is something, but not as much as people think. At work I'd say let's all know the plan by next spring. To friends I'd say I'm not against the change, but nobody should be left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd hold on until about 2030 if I'm lucky. I'd be 62, and I'd probably be moved sideways before I'm moved out. The trouble is my pension would be small and my savings would still be nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start saving in earnest, 60 a week, by cutting out the pub and the paper subscription. I'd ask Gary about a move to the trade counter. And I'd check what the council offers for older workers, because there must be something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels uncomfortable but not hopeless. With five years I can do something, though I'm not sure I'll do the right thing. I'm a bit scared of getting it wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with five years that you couldn't do with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say having time changes things for the better. With two years, I'd be stunned. With five, I could finish a course, save a bit and move to the counter. But I'd still be doing it all with no safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move to the counter. What would you give up by doing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robots coming three years later suit me. The counter and the stockroom are hands-on, and those would be safer a bit longer. My plan is to get off the screen and onto the floor before the thinking part arrives.

say: I'd say five years is something, but **not as much** as people think.
I'd ask everyone to know the **plan** by next spring.
think: I'd hold on until about **2030**, and I'd probably be moved sideways first.
My pension would be small and my **savings** still nothing.
do: **Save** 60 a week by cutting the pub and the paper subscription.
**Ask** Gary about a move to the trade counter.
**Check** what the council offers for older workers.
feel: **Uncomfortable but not hopeless**, scared of getting it wrong.
S3.quote: My plan is to get off the screen and onto the floor before the thinking part arrives.
fieldNote: He uses the three-year robot delay logically: counter and stockroom work is his **hands-on** shelter.
Still alarmed because his savings and pension are close to nothing.
More active here than in the quick picture, which shows time matters to him.

steps.text: Save 60 a week by dropping the pub and the paper subscription
Ask Gary about moving to the trade counter
Check what help the council offers older workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to get ready, if somebody bothers. At work I'd keep my head down. To friends I'd say it's the young ones who need guidance, because I'll be gone from work by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be 68 in 2036, so I'd have finished before it hits. My worry is whether there's enough in the pension. A state pension on its own would mean a very plain life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work until 65 or 66 and save what I can, say 50 a week. I'd stay at Northgate on the counter if they'd have me. And I'd tell Theo and my daughter Annick to learn something with their hands that machines can't do for a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels less heavy. I'm still not happy, but I'm not frightened for myself. I'd feel bad for the next generation, who have to live through the real change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your daughter Annick about her bank job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Annick works in a bank branch. I'd say to her: get out of the screen jobs soon. I'd say it kindly, because she's proud of her job, but I think the sooner she moves the better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a decent retirement look like for you and Maureen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What helps with ten years is that I can have my retirement without the rush. In the two-year picture I'd be pushed out, but here I'd get to leave on my own feet with a small pot and a handshake.

say: I'd say ten years is **enough** to get ready, if somebody bothers.
I'd tell friends the **young ones** need guidance, because I'll be gone by then.
think: I'd be 68 in 2036, so I'd have **finished** before it hits.
My worry is whether the **pension** is enough for more than a plain life.
do: **Work** until 65 or 66 and save 50 a week.
**Stay** at Northgate on the counter if they'll have me.
**Tell** my children to learn a hands-on skill.
feel: **Less heavy**, not frightened for myself but sorry for the next generation.
S4.quote: I'd get to leave on my own feet with a small pot and a handshake.
fieldNote: The longer horizon takes the fear out of his own job, but **pension** worries keep him anxious.
He turns to advising his children, particularly Annick at the bank.
Contrasts clearly with the two-year picture: pushed out versus leaving on his terms.

steps.text: Save 50 a week until I retire at 65 or 66
Stay at Northgate on the trade counter as long as they'll have me
Tell Annick to move out of screen-based bank work soon

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no doubt. Two years is no time at all, I'm 58 and I have nothing set aside, and there are only a couple of other parts firms for a long way round. I'd be out, and I'd have nowhere to go.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not against change. I'm against being told about it after it's been decided. If someone had asked me a year ago, I'd have said let's try it slowly and see.

headlineQuote: I'm not against change. I'm against being told about it after it's been decided.
portrait: Jamal is 58, a junior buyer at **Northgate Auto Parts**, with a partner in care-home work and two grown children.
He is **resistant** to new tools, uses a paper catalogue and has never touched AI.
He is a pragmatist in the **centre**, blaming the market and bosses a little each rather than one side.
He grows **alarmed** quickly, since his job is thinking work and his savings are nothing.
His plan is to move to the **trade counter**, which robots would reach later, and to ask his children for help.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because two years is too short and no other parts firm is nearby.
whatWouldHelp: A **date and a figure** from his boss, honest planning, and some pension help if he has to leave early.
